title: Memory layout
summary: Where a program's bytes live: text, data, BSS, heap and stack, static and thread-local storage, and stack versus heap.

clips.title: Five segments
clips.question: Where do a program's code, globals, allocations and locals live?

scenes.say: Memory layout, question one. Where do a program's code, its globals, its heap allocations, and its local variables live? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: Where do code, globals, allocations and locals live?

scenes.say: Picture one process's address space, low addresses at the bottom. The text segment holds machine code: read only, and shared between processes running the same binary. Globals and statics with a non zero initial value live in data, and that value is stored in the executable. Zero initialized ones live in BSS: the file records only the size, and the loader maps zeroed pages. The heap holds what new allocates, managed by the allocator. And each thread has its own stack, for locals and call frames. The main stack sits near the top, and grows down.

steps.note: Non-zero initial value: stored in the binary
Zero-initialized: only the size is recorded
new / malloc: managed by the allocator
One stack per thread: locals, call frames
Stack grows down; the heap grows up

clips.title: Static storage
clips.question: Why does one non-zero element make a big global array bloat the binary?

scenes.say: Question two. Two global arrays of a million ints. One makes the executable four megabytes bigger, the other costs nothing. Why? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: Why does one global array bloat the binary, and the other not?

scenes.say: A global with a value goes in data, and the value is stored in the binary. Without an initializer, or with all zeros, it goes in BSS, which costs no file space at all. But a single non zero element puts the whole four megabyte array into data. A string literal lives in read only data. Thread local gives every thread its own copy. A function local static has static storage too, but it's constructed the first time control reaches it, and that's thread safe since C++ eleven. Locals live in the stack frame. The unique pointer itself is on the stack, while its four megabytes are on the heap.

props.title: Where each variable lives
props.code:
int limit = 100;                // .data: the value is stored in the binary
int counter;                    // .bss: zero-filled at load, no file space
int zeros[1'000'000] = {};      // .bss too: an all-zero initializer
int ones[1'000'000] = {1};      // .data: ~4 MB in the executable
const char* msg = "hi";         // pointer in .data, "hi" in .rodata
thread_local int tls_hits;      // one copy per thread

Config& config() {
    static Config c = load();   // static storage, built on the first call,
    return c;                   // thread-safe since C++11
}

void f() {
    int local = 0;                               // stack frame
    auto p = std::make_unique<int[]>(1 << 20);   // 4 MB on the heap
}

highlights.note: Zero / none → .bss: free in the file
One non-zero element → all of it in .data
Literal in .rodata; thread_local: one per thread
Stack frame: the local and the unique_ptr; heap: its 4 MB

clips.title: Stack or heap?
clips.question: When should an object live on the stack, and when on the heap?

scenes.say: Question three. When should an object live on the stack, and when on the heap? Pause and answer out loud.

Allocating on the stack is just moving the stack pointer, and it's freed automatically at scope exit. But it's small: typically eight megabytes for the main thread on Linux, one on Windows. The heap goes through the allocator: bookkeeping, sometimes a lock or a system call, and fragmentation over time. It's big, and an object lives until it's freed, so own it with R A I I. Small, fixed size, short lived objects go on the stack.

props.title: Bump a pointer, or ask an allocator

left.label: Stack
left.title: Fast, automatic, small
left.body: One pointer bump; freed at scope exit. ~8 MB main thread (Linux), ~1 MB (Windows).

right.label: Heap
right.title: Flexible, slower
right.body: Allocator bookkeeping, maybe a lock or syscall, fragmentation. Lives until freed: use RAII.

verdict.text: Small, fixed-size, short-lived → stack. Big or long-lived → heap, owned by RAII.

scenes.say: And the four classic bugs. A huge local array, or deep recursion, overflows the stack. Returning the address of a local leaves a dangling pointer. Forgetting to free leaks. And touching memory after delete is use after free. Address sanitizer catches the last three.

To recap. Code is in text, initialized globals in data, zeroed ones in BSS. Function statics are built on first use, safely. The stack is fast but small, the heap is big but managed. And let R A I I own everything on the heap.

items.text: text: code · data: initialized · bss: zeroed.
Function statics: built on first use, thread-safe.
Stack: fast but small. Heap: big but managed.
Let RAII own every heap allocation.
